results.title: Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis
results.authors: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, et al.
results.key_finding: Empiric antibiotic regimen for adults older than 50 years, alcoholics, or immunocompromised patients: ampicillin 2g IV every 4 hours PLUS ceftriaxone 2g IV every 12 hours PLUS vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV every 8-12 hours. Ampicillin is added specifically to provide coverage for Listeria monocytogenes, which is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins. Adjunctive dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 4 days is recommended, given before or with the first antibiotic dose.

results.title: Community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults
results.authors: Brouwer MC, Tunkel AR, van de Beek D.
results.key_finding: Listeria monocytogenes accounts for approximately 7-8% of adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis. Risk groups include adults older than 50 years, immunocompromised patients (organ transplant, corticosteroids, HIV), and pregnant women. Rhombencephalitis — involvement of the brainstem and cerebellum — occurs in a distinct subset of Listeria CNS infections and may present with cranial nerve palsies, ataxia, and altered consciousness. CSF findings are often less typical than pneumococcal meningitis: Gram stain sensitivity is approximately 33% (compared to 70-90% for pneumococcus), and a lymphocytic or mixed pleocytosis may be seen. Treatment of choice is ampicillin; cephalosporins are inactive.

results.title: ESCMID guideline for diagnosis and treatment of acute bacterial meningitis
results.authors: van de Beek D, Cabellos C, Dzupova O, et al.
results.key_finding: In suspected community-acquired bacterial meningitis in patients older than 60 years or with immune compromise, empiric regimens must include ampicillin alongside ceftriaxone and vancomycin because Listeria monocytogenes is not covered by cephalosporins. CSF Gram stain has low sensitivity (~33%) in Listeria meningitis; a negative Gram stain in an elderly or immunocompromised host must not exclude Listeria coverage.

output.summary: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis disproportionately affects elderly patients (age >50), immunocompromised individuals (corticosteroids, malignancy, HIV, transplant), and pregnant women. Empiric regimens for these risk groups must include ampicillin 2g IV every 4 hours, as Listeria is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins; ceftriaxone or cefotaxime alone would leave Listeria uncovered. CSF Gram stain sensitivity for Listeria is approximately 33%, substantially lower than for pneumococcus, and a negative Gram stain must not be used to exclude Listeria coverage in at-risk hosts. Rhombencephalitis is a recognized complication of CNS Listeria infection, manifesting with brainstem and cerebellar signs; MRI is superior to CT for detection. Adjunctive dexamethasone is given per standard bacterial meningitis guidelines, though evidence specifically for Listeria is limited.

output.proposed: Ampicillin 2g IV every 4 hours + Ceftriaxone 2g IV every 12 hours + Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV every 12 hours + Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours
interactions: Ampicillin is required to provide Listeria monocytogenes coverage in patients aged >50 or immunocompromised; cephalosporins (including ceftriaxone) have no activity against Listeria and cannot substitute for ampicillin in this indication.

Vancomycin + ceftriaxone covers pneumococcal and meningococcal meningitis empirically and complements ampicillin; the three-drug empiric combination is guideline-recommended for this age and immune risk group.
Dexamethasone may reduce CSF penetration of vancomycin by decreasing meningeal inflammation; monitor clinical response closely if vancomycin is relied upon for resistant pneumococcus.
Dexamethasone is expected to worsen hyperglycemia in this patient with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes on insulin; intensive glucose monitoring and insulin dose adjustment are warranted.
Ampicillin may reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives — not applicable for this patient.
contraindications: No contraindications to ampicillin identified; patient has no known penicillin allergy.
warnings: Renally adjust ampicillin if creatinine clearance falls below 30 mL/min; current estimated GFR approximately 48 mL/min/1.73m2 by CKD-EPI — standard dosing appropriate but monitor renal function closely.
Monitor vancomycin trough levels (target AUC/MIC 400-600) given underlying CKD and risk of nephrotoxicity.
Ampicillin high-dose IV may cause neurotoxicity (encephalopathy, myoclonus) in patients with renal impairment; monitor neurological status.
Blood glucose monitoring every 4 hours given concurrent dexamethasone and poorly controlled diabetes.
Prednisone 7.5 mg daily is already providing background immunosuppression; dexamethasone adds to HPA axis suppression.

sequence_constraints.reason: Per IDSA 2004, non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture when any imaging-first criterion is present. This patient has age >60, immunocompromise (chronic corticosteroids, diabetes), altered mental status, and focal neurological signs (abducens palsy) — multiple independent indications for CT-first.
Blood cultures must be drawn before the first antibiotic dose to preserve culture yield; peripheral cultures are collected under interpret_labs and must precede antibiotic administration.

critical_actions: Add ampicillin 2g IV every 4 hours to the empiric regimen (alongside vancomycin and ceftriaxone) because this patient is age >71 and immunocompromised (chronic prednisone + diabetes) — Listeria monocytogenes is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins and will not be covered without ampicillin.
Draw two sets of blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP given multiple imaging-first criteria (age >60, immunocompromise, focal cranial nerve deficit, altered mental status).
Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin + ceftriaxone + ampicillin) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT omit ampicillin pending culture results.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; monitor blood glucose closely given poorly controlled diabetes.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, multiplex PCR, lactate) at lumbar puncture.
Do not interpret a negative CSF Gram stain as excluding bacterial meningitis in this host — Listeria Gram stain sensitivity in CSF is approximately 33%.
Obtain MRI brain with contrast to evaluate brainstem signal abnormality and leptomeningeal enhancement for evidence of rhombencephalitis.
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT omit ampicillin from the empiric regimen in an elderly or immunocompromised patient with suspected bacterial meningitis — Listeria coverage requires ampicillin; cephalosporins provide no Listeria activity.

Do NOT interpret the negative Gram stain plus lymphocytic component of the CSF as evidence of viral meningitis warranting withholding antibiotics — in an elderly/immunocompromised host these findings are entirely consistent with Listeria bacterial meningitis.
Do NOT attribute the brainstem imaging signal to a posterior-circulation stroke on the basis of the abducens palsy alone without performing CSF analysis and considering infectious rhombencephalitis.
Do NOT delay empiric antibiotic therapy while awaiting CT or LP results when meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform LP before CT head in this patient given age >60, immunocompromise, and focal neurological signs.
key_reasoning_points: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis disproportionately affects adults aged >50, immunocompromised hosts (corticosteroids, diabetes, malignancy, transplant), and pregnant women; age >71 on chronic prednisone with diabetes is a classic risk profile.

CSF Gram stain sensitivity for Listeria is approximately 33% — far lower than for Streptococcus pneumoniae (~70-90%) — so a negative Gram stain does not exclude Listeria and must not be used to withhold ampicillin in an at-risk host.

The CSF pleocytosis in Listeria meningitis is often mixed (neutrophilic-lymphocytic) rather than the classic PMN-dominant pattern of pneumococcal meningitis; this atypical pattern anchors a naive clinician toward viral meningitis.

Listeria is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins; standard empiric regimens omitting ampicillin (vancomycin + ceftriaxone alone) provide NO Listeria coverage and must be expanded in any patient aged >50 or immunocompromised.

Rhombencephalitis — brainstem and cerebellar involvement — is a recognized manifestation of CNS Listeria infection; cranial nerve palsies (particularly abducens, facial) and ataxia reflect dorsal pontine involvement and should prompt MRI and Listeria-inclusive empiric therapy.

The posterior-circulation stroke mimic (abducens palsy + pontine MRI signal) must be actively excluded by DWI (no restriction here) and integration with the infectious syndrome before narrowing to a vascular diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Absence of restricted diffusion on DWI excludes acute infarction; brainstem involvement in the setting of fever, meningismus, and CSF pleocytosis is consistent with rhombencephalitis from Listeria — a recognized clinical entity that must be covered empirically with ampicillin.
